title: The dawn recitation
hookLine: the recitation at dawn is witnessed (17:78–79)

cards: There's a particular quiet before sunrise. The street hasn't started. Phones haven't buzzed.

The sky goes from black to a deep blue that lasts only a few minutes. In homes all over the world, at that hour, someone stands on a prayer mat reciting, by tradition longer than at any other prayer of the day.
Al-Isra has a verse about that hour, and it makes a claim about who else is there.

teach.b: Verse seventy-eight lays out a day of prayer: from the sun's decline after noon to the dark of night, and then the Qur'an at dawn.

Commentators read the times of the five daily prayers in that one sentence, with the dawn prayer, Fajr, named last and on its own. Then, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! (the recital of) the Qur'an at dawn is ever witnessed."
Mashhud: witnessed, attended. By whom? A hadith in Bukhari answers.

teach.h: TWO SHIFTS OF ANGELS AT DAWN.
teach.b: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said the angels of the night and the angels of the day gather at the dawn prayer: one shift going off, one coming on.
The companion Abu Hurayrah, after relating it, would say: recite, if you like, the Qur'an at dawn is ever witnessed.
So in the hadith's picture, the dawn recitation is a handover, and whoever is praying stands in the middle of it.

Verse seventy-nine adds the night: keep a vigil with it, an extra gift, and perhaps your Lord will raise you to a praised station. That's the root of tahajjud, the optional late-night prayer some Muslims keep.

teach.h: THE QUR'AN AT DAWN IS EVER WITNESSED.
teach.b: This week ran from patience given by God, through a night journey, a sigh held back for a parent, a hand neither tied nor flung open, a claim checked before it's repeated, and the spirit beyond our little knowledge.
Al-Isra opened in the dark of one night. For us, it closes at first light.

how: Muslims pray Fajr before sunrise, traditionally with a longer recitation than the other prayers; some also keep tahajjud, a voluntary night prayer, in the last part of the night.

practice: Choose something short to recite: the Fatiha, a verse from this week, or any line that matters to you, and say it now, slowly, once.
Then picture the morning: the dark window, the quiet, and you saying it before the day starts talking, at Fajr if you pray, or with your first glass of water if you don't.
